result.white_space:
The proposed core (evidence dossier, draft petition, fixed-fee advocate, WhatsApp funnel, Rs 3,000-8,000) is already sold by many advocates and by LegalFund, and the price is not differentiated. Some competitors undercut it with success-fee pricing (Online Legal Center, LegalFund). A Rs 499 template pack exists. Expect to fight for the same 'account frozen' search traffic against SEO-heavy advocate sites, and expect the free MHA/CFCFRMS grievance route and HC-mandated timelines to resolve some low-value cases without a lawyer.

What appears unserved, since no funded product-led competitor turned up in any search:
(1) Software, not lawyers. No one automates extraction of the flagged credit, payer VPA, invoice match and merchant vintage from a bank statement or UPI settlement data into an investigating-officer-ready bundle. Competitors sell PDFs and lawyer time.
(2) Group and B2B buyers. The pain is concentrated in identifiable bodies, such as the Tamil Nadu Petroleum Dealers Association (about 5,000 outlets threatening to stop UPI) and CA firms. No one sells them a standing response desk.
(3) SLA-tracking and escalation against the new SOP clocks (7-day bank upload, 15-day investigating officer, 90-day hold, HC 3-month limit). This is a workflow-tracking gap that solo advocates do not productize.
(4) Prevention and continuity (order-ID dynamic QR, per-payment invoice, sweep or separate collections account). Nobody was found selling this to small merchants.

Weak or risky parts of the idea:
- Rs 199/month 'Merchant Shield': no evidence anyone pays to pre-empt a freeze that may never come.
- NBFC bridge advance against a frozen balance: the balance is under a police lien and no lender product was found. Treat it as unproven.
- Advocate network with a fixed split: Bar Council of India Rule 36 (solicitation and advertising) has been enforced against online platforms. BCI sent cease-and-desist notices to Justdial, Sulekha and Quikr, and the Supreme Court has issued notice on the issue. A platform that takes a cut of advocate fees or generates leads is the exact structure at risk.
- Market shrinkage: MHA SOP, Rajasthan HC statewide guidelines (20 Aug 2026), Allahabad HC, MP HC and the AP HC ruling are pushing banks toward lien-only holds. The small-sum tail is largely solved by regulation if enforced. The remaining paid pain is whole-account freezes and higher balances.

result.kill_reason: n/a. The advocate-plus-dossier service layer is crowded, but credible white space remains. result.sharper_angle:
Drop the consumer lawyer marketplace, because that is the crowded layer and the risky one under BCI Rule 36. Build merchant-side freeze-response software sold through trade bodies, CA firms and UPI acceptance providers.

1. Product: connect UPI settlement or bank-statement data. When a freeze notice or lien lands, auto-build the investigating-officer and nodal-officer bundle (flagged credit, payer VPA, matching invoice or order ID, merchant vintage and turnover history). File it through the free CFCFRMS grievance route, and use it for Gujarat-style state portals where they exist.
2. SLA engine: track the SOP clocks (bank 7 days, investigating officer 15 days, 90-day hold) and the AP, Rajasthan, Allahabad and MP HC directions. Auto-escalate to district and state grievance officers. Recommend a writ only when a deadline is missed or the whole account is frozen.
3. Advocates: the merchant hires an independent advocate directly, or a law-firm partner does the work under its own engagement. The company charges a software or subscription fee, not a fee-share or lead-gen cut, to stay clear of BCI Rule 36.
4. Buyers: sell to associations first (petrol dealers, trader federations, CA networks). The Tamil Nadu Petroleum Dealers Association's 5,000 outlets are an obvious first test. Offer a group plan, a common template and group filings modelled on Rajasthan's 105-petition bundle.
5. Target segment: whole-account freezes and disputed sums above about Rs 50,000. Under the SOP, smaller freezes auto-lift at day 90, so the software and advocate fee is worth it mainly for larger current accounts.
6. Later B2B: sell 'freeze-ready' evidence capture (order-ID dynamic QR, invoice per payment) to QR, soundbox and PSP providers and bank merchant-onboarding teams, who want fewer over-freeze complaints.
7. Defer the NBFC bridge advance and the Rs 199 Merchant Shield subscription until case data shows willingness to pay.

Validation before building: run a 20-case pilot with one association and one law firm. Measure time to lien release versus the advocate-only baseline, and confirm merchants will pay for prevention.

result.white_space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Strong on policy pull and on the problem, thin on proof anyone pays for the exact bundle.
- Regulators are writing developer-funded independent monitoring into rules. Franklin County, IN draft ordinance: developer-paid real-time monitoring wells, a licensed-hydrogeologist impact assessment, and an escrow for 24-hour potable water to impacted neighbors (https://www.franklincounty.in.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Data-Center-Regulations-Draft-v3.0-03.30.26-1.pdf and https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8103901/indiana/franklin-county/franklin-county-workgroup-seeks-strict-water-protections-for-proposed-data-centers). Shenandoah County, VA officials back independent third-party testing funded by the applicant (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9504403/virginia/shenandoah-county/officials-ask-stronger-noise-air-quality-monitoring-and-enforcement-for-future-data-centers). St. Louis's permit requires an annual third-party noise report and a developer-funded hydraulic model study (https://www.stlouis-mo.gov/government/departments/mayor/news/data-center-permit-approved.cfm).
- A live baseline-less dispute: Meta's Newton County, GA neighbors say their wells went dry or silted up. Meta's own study says groundwater flows away from them, and families sued in Sept 2026 (https://www.ajc.com/news/2026/09/georgia-families-sue-meta-accuse-its-data-center-of-tainting-their-water/, https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2025/07/15/meta-built-a-new-data-center-in-georgia-their-neighbors-water-ran-dry/). This shows developer-commissioned studies are not believed. Cheyenne's Meta-contractor wastewater contamination led to a $10k fine (https://fortune.com/2026/07/10/wyoming-officials-meta-715000-square-foot-data-center-responsible-contaminating-water-system-rare-bacterium/).
- Developers are already spending on neighbors with no neutral mechanism, and residents reject it. NorthPoint's $10k-per-household offer ($45M) was called a bribe, with residents wanting property-value protection instead (https://reason.com/2026/09/28/data-centers-and-their-discontents/, https://propmodo.com/cash-to-residents-is-the-newest-tool-in-the-data-center-fight/). Propmodo expects future versions to be 'tied to utility bill credits or property value guarantees rather than lump sums'. The Mason County developer offers buyouts at the highest of three independent valuations plus a premium, with no independent oversight (https://wchstv.com/news/local/voluntary-buyout-offers-rolled-out-for-meadowlands-estates-homes-near-data-center).
- Precedent that baseline mandates create a paid vendor category: Pennsylvania Act 13 (oil and gas) makes operators pay third-party pre-drill water tests for wells within 1,000 ft, and a rebuttable presumption of liability applies when no baseline exists (https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dep/programs-and-services/oil-and-gas/related-topics/act-13/act-13-faq). No equivalent presumption exists yet for data centers, so developers currently lack a legal reason to buy.
- The 'why now' facts check out. NY Executive Order 62, July 14, 2026, pauses DEC discretionary permits for 50 MW+ data centers (https://www.dwt.com/blogs/energy--environmental-law-blog/2026/07/ny-data-center-permitting-pause-executive-order-62). Texas ordered TCEQ to halt data-center permits on Sept 21, 2026 (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/21/texas-governor-abbott-ai-data-center-permits.html). Reuters/Ipsos: 14% comfortable with a data center nearby, 57% opposed (https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/articles/2026-06-11/americans-wary-of-ai-driven-data-center-boom-reuters-ipsos-poll-shows). I could not verify the 'local pauses in at least 14 states' claim.
- Vendor signals (marketing, not proof of spend): KETOS's 'missing baseline' pitch (https://ketos.co/data-centers-water-quality) and a groundwater-marketing blog saying monitoring and hydrogeology services are 'being specified in RFPs right now' (https://groundwatermarketing.com/blog/data-centers-groundwater-demand/).
- Not found: any developer or county publicly paying a neutral party for a parametric neighbor payout, or any RFP for one.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not sell 'Baseline-in-a-Box' as a sensor product, because KETOS, Aethair, Envirosuite and the developer-hired consultancies already cover it and it will commoditize. Sell neutral trusteeship of a neighbor-protection covenant, starting with well water only.

1. Be the escrow and trust administrator plus an independent technical panel, with governance the county co-approves. Buy commodity sensors and labs from KETOS, Kunak or Eno Scientific-type vendors instead of competing with them.
2. Lead with a well-drawdown guarantee, because dry or silted wells drive the lawsuits and hearings (Meta Newton County). Fix the attribution problem in the trigger design. Use upgradient control wells, pumping records and a difference-versus-control test, so the developer pays only for excess drawdown and not for drought. Bring in an MGA or carrier partner for capacity so the payout is legally clean and does not run into state insurance law.
3. Sell it to counties as a ready-made permit-condition and development-agreement template, aimed first at jurisdictions already drafting escrow-for-neighbors language (Franklin County, IN; Shenandoah, VA). The county mandates it, the developer funds it, and you skip the developer's reluctance to volunteer a payout.
4. Add noise, PM2.5 and voltage as paid extensions later. Enroll per household instead of pricing bespoke $75-150k builds.

First proof to get: one county or developer willing to put the guarantee escrow in writing, and a counsel opinion on whether the structure is insurance. If neither exists within about 90 days, the idea collapses into the crowded monitoring market and should be dropped.

result.white_space:
Coverage caveat: the WebSearch quota (200 per session) was already used up when I started, so I could not run the planned 6-12 searches. I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Do a manual pass on those before committing.

What I found: I found no productized, US-facing service that bundles (a) a serialized tool census, (b) cavity-level physical fingerprints, and (c) marketplace test-buy attribution of overruns to a specific tool. The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. Marketplace monitoring and takedown (Red Points, Corsearch, Alibaba's free IP platform) is commoditized and crowded. Object fingerprinting exists (Alitheon) but is aimed at electronics, aerospace and gray-market diversion, not tool-mark attribution.

Genuinely unserved: (1) cavity-level 'which tool made this part' attribution that holds up as evidence; (2) a tooling census standard for mid-market OEMs, timed to the exit window; (3) an evidence pack designed for counsel that a brand-protection vendor's screenshot-and-takedown workflow does not produce.

Attribution is legally useful only when the overrun carries the client's IP (trademark, design patent, trade dress) and the client can enforce it. result.sharper_angle: Drop 'ghost parcels' as the headline and lead with large-commercial-meter revenue assurance. result.white_space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). San Diego's court page states 'the court is prohibited by law from allowing remote court reporting for any court proceeding' (https://sdcourt.ca.gov/sdcourt/generalinformation/resourcelists/courtreporterinformation). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind.
result.evidence_of_demand:

Problem scale:
- More than 3 million civil, family and probate hearings had no verbatim record from April 2023 to March 2026 (Law360 https://www.law360.com/pulse/courts/articles/2529851; CalMatters https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/court-reporter-california-supreme-court/).

- FVAP's shortage page says the lack of a record makes appeals 'practically impossible' (https://fvaplaw.org/court-reporter-shortage/).

Price pain:
- Private pro tem costs run about $450-500 for a half day, and a trial reporter costs about $3,300 per day (Law360, KALW https://www.kalw.org/bay-area-news/2026-08-13/california-supreme-court-rules-that-courts-must-allow-electronic-recordings-of-hearings, StenoScout https://stenoscout.com/blog/how-much-does-court-reporter-cost/).
- Courts tell family litigants 'There will be no court reporter available. If you want the case reported, you will need to make arrangements for your own' (Sacramento https://www.saccourt.ca.gov/court-reporters/court-reporters.aspx).
- Some counties charge only $30 for under one hour of an official reporter (San Bernardino fee schedule), which shows how far below market the subsidized price sits.

Regulation forcing spend:
- FVAP v. Superior Court, S288176 (Aug 10, 2026) holds courts have a mandatory duty to give indigent litigants an official verbatim record on request, including 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' or electronic recording (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2026/s288176.html; https://fvaplaw.org/case-alert-fvap-et-al-v-superior-courts-et-al-2026-california-courts-have-a-mandatory-duty-to-provide-a-verbatim-record-of-all-court-proceedings-for-parties-who-cannot-afford-to-pay-for-a-privat/).
- Courts pay under that ruling, not legal aid credits, and the Chief Justice wrote that 'a verbatim record created by electronic recording is better than no record at all'. The cheap fallback is recording, not a reporter.

Demand not found: no RFP, forum thread or paid pilot showing attorneys or litigants will pay about $95 per hearing. The idea itself concedes 'nobody pays that for a routine hearing' at today's price. The only market signals for cheaper on-demand reporters are deposition-side products (DirectDep, Steno Job Marketplace).

Code 69959), so the idea as written cannot launch without a legislative change or a court-run structure.
result.sharper_angle: Drop the private remote-dispatch model for California, because Gov. Code 69959 bars remote reporting outside court-employed pilot reporters in a court facility. Build one of two versions instead. (A) Courthouse-hopping pro tem service. Reporters are physically present and cover 6-10 family departments in one big courthouse, using the calendar-duration prediction. Sell a flat per-hearing fee to attorneys, and sell pay-per-department-day capacity to courts as a lawful way to meet the FVAP mandate with 'pro tem reporters paid by the court'. (B) Scheduling and utilization software for courts and their AB 3013 remote pilots, meaning reporter-to-calendar matching, dead-time reduction and retention analytics, sold B2G to the 13 pilot counties. Pair either with a certified-transcript upsell on court electronic recordings (the eScribers model, priced for appeals) so revenue survives courts shifting to audio. Alternatively, launch first in a state that allows remote reporting by private reporters, where the mechanic is legal and the same shortage exists, and come back to California if the legislature opens it. Before spending money, run a one-week legal check (Judicial Council, and a court reporter licensing attorney) on whether any local rule lets a pro tem attend a video family hearing remotely.

result.white_space:
The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Real but soft and mostly supply-side. I found no RFPs, forum complaints from named small makers, or published customer counts.

Regulatory push (strong):
- Article 14 reporting applied from 11 Sep 2026 and the ENISA SRP went live the same day. Fines run up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. See https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/its-live-the-cyber-resilience-act-reporting-is-mandatory-as-of-today-11-september-2026 and https://cra-facts.com/penalties.
- Law-firm and press coverage stresses that firms need a PSIRT-like process and that 24h is tight. See https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/09/11/eus-cyber-resilience-act-starts-the-24-hour-vulnerability-clock/5295821 (which says the pain is supply-chain visibility, not staffing), https://startupfortune.com/eus-cyber-resilience-act-now-requires-24-hour-hack-reporting/ and https://www.fisherphillips.com/en/insights/insights/eu-cyber-resilience-act-reporting-is-now-live.
- An ENISA survey reported via a Mondaq/UpGuard search result found 66% of SME respondents had heard of the CRA and one in five were unsure it applied to them.

Vendors are already building for it:
- Finite State markets its managed service to teams with 'one or two people in product security, or no dedicated function' (https://finitestate.io/blog/cra-compliance-is-a-full-time-job).
- TridentSec sells a PSIRT-as-a-Service retainer (https://tridentsec.eu/services/psirt-consulting/).
- Patchstack launched free managed Article 14 filing for OSS on day one (https://patchstack.com/articles/launching-managed-cra-article-14-reporting-for-open-source-maintainers/).
- CRACI raised a EUR 1.4M pre-seed for CRA automation (https://arcticstartup.com/craci-raises-e1-4-million-pre-seed/).

Price anchors:
- EcoComply charges from EUR 1,500 per product category per year for an authorised-representative mandate covering Article 14 (https://ecocomply.ai/blog/cra-reporting-obligations-non-eu-manufacturers).
- CVD Portal charges EUR 99-299/mo for software (https://cvdportal.com/pricing).
- Outsourced-DPO services are a comparable model at EUR 1,500-5,000/mo mid-range (https://www.engagecompliance.co/outsourced-dpo-cost-guide).
- Regulus's calculator estimates only 16-32 hours (about EUR 1.4-2.7k) of internal effort to set up vulnerability handling and reporting readiness (https://goregulus.com/resources/cra-cost-calculator/). That suggests many small firms will do it in-house at low cost.

No evidence found that anyone pays EUR 1,500-6,000/mo for a filing desk today, because the regime is only 17 days old.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not launch as a generic 'PSIRT retainer'. TridentSec, Finite State, Cybellum and the consultancies already own that framing, and CVD Portal has pushed software-only reporting down to EUR 99/mo. Launch instead as the 24/7 Article 14 filing desk for non-EU connected-device brands, with three changes.

1. Bundle the AR mandate with the filing SLA. Be the named SRP Assigned Representative plus EU authorised-representative mandate, with a written guarantee such as 'triage decision within 4h, early warning filed inside 24h including weekends'. That is the one deliverable competitors avoid because filing is 'customer-owned'. Price it as a low base fee (EUR 300-800/mo or EUR 2-4k/yr per product family, anchored to EcoComply's EUR 1,500/yr AR price) plus a per-incident fee (EUR 1-3k). Do not price it at EUR 1,500-6,000/mo up front.

2. Pool the triage by shared component stack, not by client. Specialise in a few stacks that many small makers share: ESP-IDF/ESP32, OpenWrt/Qualcomm and Realtek router SDKs, Zephyr, Tuya and Matter modules, and Yocto Linux. An actively exploited entry in one SDK then gets analysed once and fanned out to 30-100 clients as pre-approved VEX and notice drafts. That is where the 30-clients-per-analyst economics come from, and it is hard for one-off consultancies to copy.

3. Sell through channels that carry the liability, not to the makers directly. Target EU importers and marketplace sellers, ODM/contract manufacturers, and chip and module vendors' ecosystems. Also offer white-label wholesale 24/7 back-end capacity to TUV, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas, TridentSec and the SBOM platforms, so incumbents become distributors, not rivals.

Sequencing: sell the audit and drill first as the lead product, since reporting-readiness is what regulators and customers will ask for. Treat the monthly filing desk as the recurring add-on, and expect it to sell mainly to firms above the small-enterprise fine exemption (50+ staff or over EUR 10M turnover). Move fast: Patchstack shows platforms can ship managed filing within days, so the window before this becomes a checkbox feature is probably 6-12 months. Before committing, get a professional-indemnity quote and confirm with ENISA or a CSIRT that an external firm can serve as AR using personal EU Login accounts.

(1) UFAA requires a Certificate of Confirmation of Grant (High Court) or a Public Trustee summary administration certificate before beneficiaries can claim a deceased person's unclaimed assets, and beneficiary claims take up to 90 days versus 30 for owners: https://www.ufaa.go.ke/claiming-instructions/ and https://www.ufaa.go.ke/faqs/. That avoids competing with advocates and with Ardhisasa or e-filing. (3) Start with cohorts that share one registry and chief: members of the same 1960s-80s land-buying company or settlement scheme in one county. Batch searches and field trips give better unit economics than single estates. (4) Keep the SACCO and coop B2B lane as a second channel, sold as cleared-estate throughput. (5) Treat asset discovery as a flat add-on, since UFAA claims need a confirmed grant first. That makes it an upsell after succession, not a lead product. (6) Before building, do the searches I could not run: Kenyan legal-tech startups, land-buying-company succession help desks, diaspora land-services firms, and whether Ardhisasa handles transmission by succession end-to-end.

result.white_space:
Verdict is a 'gap' with moderate confidence. I found no product or startup that sells remote-RN witnessing of controlled-substance waste, or a remote-RN transfusion or high-alert double-check, as a narrow night-shift service for critical access hospitals. Two related searches (a narrow 'remote/virtual witness waste' query and a startup-plus-diversion query) returned zero such vendors. What exists is broad virtual-nursing platforms and telepharmacy (Caregility, NESA, Artisight, LookDeep, VitalChat, Avel eCare, Cardinal). Some of these list 'second signature / medication verification' as a feature. Their sales motion is a large virtual-care program with a hospital or health system, not a $1,500/month drop-in night witness with a $150 cart and PDF audit log for a 25-bed hospital. Unserved wedge: the waste-witness event itself, with time-stamped video matched to cabinet waste records for the diversion committee, sold with an insurer angle.

Threats to the wedge:
1) Caregility, VitalChat and telepharmacy vendors (Avel, Cardinal) already have remote clinicians on video and rural relationships, and could add witnessing as a feature.
2) Legal risk is the biggest unknown. 21 CFR 1317.95 requires 'two employees of the registrant' to 'personally witness' destruction (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/1317.95). That rule is written for inventory destruction and I could not confirm whether it governs patient-dose waste. A contracted third-party remote RN might not count as an employee or as 'personally' present. State boards vary and I did not check any. Medical Solutions says 'in most states any licensed nurse or pharmacist can be a witness' and stresses direct in-person observation.
3) A camera at the cabinet proves the waste happened on camera. It does not prove the syringe contents (swap or saline substitution), which is the gap that waste-testing vendors address.
4) Hospitals may prefer barcode or electronic transfusion verification, or a remote pharmacist, over a new vendor.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before my first query. I ran a handful of search-engine result pages through WebFetch (Brave and Bing) and stopped after rate limiting. I did not scrape further. I therefore did NOT check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch, open-source tools, state board rules, RFPs or RHTP funding notices. I also could not fetch Cactus Smart Sink (a camera-equipped waste-sink product I recall but could not verify), Omnicell or BD Pyxis pages. Someone should check those before committing.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Demand for the problem is well evidenced. Willingness to pay for this specific service is not.

Problem evidence:
- American Nurse Journal: 'drug diversion most commonly occurs during wasting', and 'frequently asking colleagues to sign off on waste they didn't witness' is a listed red flag. It advises documenting 'not visualized' in the cabinet comment field (https://www.myamericannurse.com/drug-diversion-in-healthcare/).
- Bluesight: staff exploit the 'waste buddy' system in an 'overworked and understaffed' environment, and '66% of hospitals surveyed' experience diversion (https://www.bluesight.com/news/drug-waste-often-equals-drug-diversion/ and https://www.bluesight.com/). I could not verify the idea's 63% figure.
- Minnesota Hospital Association security material, seen only as a search snippet, flags 'virtual waste where another nurse signs but doesn't actually witness' (URL not fetched).

Spend on comparable remote-staffing workarounds:
- Hospitals already pay for staffed virtual nursing that includes second-signature verification (Caregility: https://caregility.com/telehealth-programs/virtual-nursing).
- They pay for 24/7 remote pharmacist coverage (Cardinal Health remote pharmacy, 'over 450 inpatient pharmacies' per its search snippet; Avel eCare, https://www.avelecare.com/).
- Rural-focused vendors are actively pitching Rural Health Transformation money (VitalChat's RHT Alliance, https://www.vitalchat.com/; Caregility, https://caregility.com/rural-health-transformation/). I did not verify RHTP dollars or that any state funds this use case.

Missing:
- No RFP, forum post or budget line found from a critical access hospital asking for a remote witness.
- No regulator guidance found that accepts remote video witnessing.
- No published pricing found for any comparable service.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not pitch 'remote second-RN' as a general service, because that is what Caregility and other virtual-nursing vendors already list. Pitch a compliance-first 'Night Verification Desk' for critical access hospitals, and start with the pieces least exposed to the DEA and state-board risk.

1) Lead with blood transfusion and high-alert drug double-checks. These are hospital-policy and P&T decisions, not DEA destruction rules. Use waste witnessing as the second step, once you hold written opinions from two or three boards.

2) Before building, get written positions from the boards of pharmacy and nursing in 2-3 telepharmacy-friendly states, such as Nebraska, Iowa, the Dakotas or Montana. Get an attorney read on whether a contracted remote RN can be the 'employee' witness under 21 CFR 1317.95.

3) Use a licensed pharmacist or RN pool. In most states a pharmacist can also witness, and remote pharmacists are already accepted in rural telepharmacy.

4) Make the artifact the product. Deliver a tamper-evident, time-stamped clip plus attestation matched to cabinet waste records, formatted for the diversion committee and the malpractice or captive insurer. Price it as risk reduction with an insurer premium credit or co-pay. Do not price it as staffing.

5) Consider selling the workflow and audit log as a white-label add-on to Avel eCare, Cardinal, VitalChat or Bluesight rather than competing with them on nurse supply. They are the likeliest fast followers and the natural distribution channel.

6) Handle the swap-off-camera weakness by pairing the camera with a waste-capture container or waste-testing step, or by partnering with a waste-testing vendor, so the video plus verified contents closes the loop.

result.white_space:
The full five-part bundle is crowded module by module: hiring-fraud IDV (Nametag, Persona and Okta/Entra partners), supplier onboarding and CMMC (Exostar, Exiger, Vanta), and ABAC and export control (NextLabs, Descartes). What I did not find is a startup-scale product that does all of the following:
1. Turns ITAR US-person status into a maintained, auditable attribute. In the ITAR sense, US person means citizen, lawful permanent resident or protected individual. Generic IDV proves a person is real and not their ITAR status, so this needs a legal-grade status determination plus an attestation.
2. Pushes that attribute through SCIM or group sync into the IdP and downstream SaaS, repos and PLM. Entra custom security attributes cannot ride in SAML or JWT claims, so a group or SCIM sync layer is a real technical gap.
3. Reconciles a person-by-person roster against actual permission lists (Drive, GitHub, PLM) and flags foreign-person exposure. I found no self-serve audit product for this. The likely alternatives are consultants and export counsel.
4. Tracks foreign-person exceptions (TAA, license or exemption) per person and per data category. Descartes covers only the visa-form piece.
NextLabs serves the prime-contractor tier and Descartes is workflow and screening software, so neither obviously targets Series A-C startups with 50-500 staff. That claim comes from limited page evidence, not pricing data.

Weaknesses of the current pitch:
- Supplier KYB, counterfeit parts and the CMMC evidence pack have entrenched owners (Exostar, Exiger, Vanta).
- Hiring-fraud and North Korean IT-worker positioning is a marketed feature of Nametag, Persona and Okta.
- The 10 Nov 2026 CMMC Phase 2 'why now' looks shaky. The Wikipedia CMMC article states that on July 13, 2026 the Pentagon temporarily paused Phase 2 and set up a CMMC Reform Task Force. That is a single source I could not corroborate, so verify it before using the date. CMMC also assesses NIST 800-171 controls, not staff nationality, so it is a weak driver for this product.
- Startups already have cheap workarounds: I-9 plus HR attestation, US-person-only tenants and enclaves, and encrypted-data carve-outs (PreVeil).
- The addressable market is small: a few hundred US space and defense-space startups.
- The company would take on legal exposure by attesting to US-person status. That needs export-counsel-approved standards.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was already exhausted when I started, so I ran no web searches. A few Bing pages fetched through WebFetch returned junk. I stopped that because using WebFetch as a search-engine workaround sidesteps the budget. The competitor list therefore comes from direct vendor-page and primary-source fetches only. Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and TechCrunch checks were not done, and I could not confirm NextLabs' Teamcenter or Windchill integrations or any competitor's funding. A small ITAR-specific startup could be missed. Run a fresh search pass before committing.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Regulatory and threat pressure is real, but I found no direct evidence that startups pay for a US-person attribute product.

Regulatory forcing function (foreign-person access is a serious violation):
- The Wikipedia ITAR article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Traffic_in_Arms_Regulations) states that sharing technical data with foreign nationals is an export requiring approval. It lists penalties including ITT $100M, General Dynamics Land Systems $20M (for letting unauthorized dual nationals from Syria and China access USML items), Space Systems/Loral $20M and Hughes $32M.

Threat pressure on hiring fraud:
- The DOJ North Korean IT worker announcement (https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-coordinated-nationwide-actions-combat-north-korean-remote) reports more than 100 US companies targeted, searches of 21 premises across 14 states and about 137 laptops seized in June 2025, and over 70 laptops recovered in October 2024.

Existing paid spend on adjacent workarounds:
- Nametag (https://getnametag.com) sells workforce IDV against North Korean IT workers to HubSpot, Reddit and Autodesk.
- PreVeil (https://www.preveil.com/itar/) claims 1,800+ customers for ITAR and CMMC tooling.
- Exostar (https://www.exostar.com) claims 200,000+ organizations and more than half of the DIB.
- Vanta (https://www.vanta.com/products/cmmc) sells CMMC Level 2 compliance.

Negative and weakening signals:
- Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cybersecurity_Maturity_Model_Certification) reports the Pentagon paused CMMC Phase 2 on July 13, 2026 as 'too bureaucratic and burdensome', with a reform task force reviewing the program. Single source, unverified.
- No forum complaints, RFPs or startup case studies about US-person attribute tooling turned up. The spend seen is on enclaves, encryption and CMMC, not on IDV-fed nationality ABAC.
result.sharper_angle:
Cut the bundle to one wedge, an 'ITAR access ledger' for space startups. Drop supplier KYB and counterfeit parts (Exostar and Exiger own it), the generic CMMC evidence pack (Exostar and Vanta), and the North Korean hiring-fraud pitch (Nametag, Persona and Okta market it). The product would:
1. Keep an attested roster of each person's ITAR status: US person, or foreign person with an authorization on file. IDV is bought from a partner, with a document-and-attestation flow for citizen, LPR and protected-individual status, built to a standard export counsel has signed off on.
2. Sync that roster into Okta and Entra groups through SCIM, working around Entra's lack of SAML and JWT claim support for custom security attributes.
3. Continuously diff the roster against real Drive, GitHub and PLM permissions and flag foreign-person exposure.
4. Track foreign-person exceptions (TAA, license or exemption) per person and per data category.

Sell the $2K ITAR access audit as a fixed-price entry offer. Go to market through space accelerators and export-control law firms, not the CMMC calendar, since the Nov 2026 date may have slipped. Position it as a complement to Exostar, Vanta, PreVeil and NextLabs, and consider selling it as an add-on through those platforms.

Before building, verify the CMMC pause and interview 10 ITAR empowered officials. Ask what they use today, whether I-9 plus attestation already satisfies their counsel, and whether they would pay for continuous roster-to-permission reconciliation. If most say attestation suffices, kill it.

result.white_space:
Caveat: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so I worked from Google News RSS headlines, Wikipedia, company homepages and the regulatory text. I could not query Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt, and Reddit and forum sites were blocked. 'No funded direct competitor found' is therefore medium-low confidence and should be re-checked before committing capital.

What looks unserved: a US-funded startup or incumbent that packages the whole sequence for orphaned import containers. That sequence is finding the box, getting the trustee's title, getting a carrier's certificate, entering it as purchaser-IOR on a single-transaction bond, screening compliance, and delivering it to an off-price buyer. Liquidators (Hilco, Gordon Brothers) hold the trustees and lenders but not the customs mechanics. Marketplaces (B-Stock, Liquidity Services, Highstock) sell goods that are already entered and free to move. Customs brokers file entries but do not source or buy distressed cargo.

Structural problems that shrink the opportunity:
1. Carriers already lien-sell resalable cargo themselves (The Loadstar), and CBP General Order sales are open to any bidder (19 CFR 127.28). The desk is only worth paying when it beats a carrier's own disposal or a wait for the auction.
2. Under 19 CFR 141.11, entry rights come from a properly endorsed negotiable bill of lading or a carrier's certificate. A non-negotiable bill cannot be endorsed to a purchaser, so carrier or NVOCC cooperation is a hard gate on every deal.
3. Abandoned cargo skews to low-value scrap (The Loadstar), so deals with real margin may be few and lumpy.
4. The 'record volumes keep yard costs high' claim is shaky. US container imports fell through 2025-26 (LA Times 'goods recession', Nov 2025; gCaptain on NRF's prolonged-decline forecast, Dec 2025), which eases congestion and demurrage pressure.
5. The FMC billing-rule lever is weaker than the idea assumes. The D.C. Circuit vacated 46 CFR 541.4, the rule limiting who may be billed (Holland & Knight, Oct 2025).
result.evidence_of_demand:
Headline-level evidence only. CNBC, Inc and Business Insider were blocked, so I could not read the articles. I found no forum threads, RFPs or price quotes showing anyone paying for a rescue desk, so willingness to pay is unproven.

Supply of orphaned cargo (tariff stress on importers):
- CNBC, Apr 9, 2025: 'Trump tariffs will lead to abandoned freight at ports as cash-strapped businesses reject orders'. Reuters via Inc, Apr 11, 2025: 'How Are Businesses Dealing With Imports Made Too Expensive by Tariffs? By Rejecting Them'. Both came up in https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=abandoned+freight+tariffs+importers&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US:en
- CNBC, Feb 12, 2026: record $3.5B US Customs bond funding shortfall from tariffs. See https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=customs+bond+funding+shortfall+importers+CNBC&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US:en
- Bankruptcy pressure: finance-commerce.com, Dec 31, 2025 ('Bankruptcies surged this year amid inflation, tariffs'). Xpert.Digital, Jan 29, 2026, on US firms filing for insolvency. A 2026 tariff-related retail bankruptcy wave also shows up in Google News, for example Eddie Bauer's operator in Feb 2026.
- Estates now hold IEEPA refund claims: refunds opened Apr 20, 2026 (CNBC 'Tariff refunds begin on Monday'), after the Supreme Court ruling of Feb 20, 2026. This supports the why-now, and it gives trustees a reason to hire someone with customs expertise.

Buyer-side demand and capital in liquidation:
- Off-price strength: Business Insider, Jan 10, 2026 ('Ross is stocking up on brands like Gucci and Hoka'); FT, Mar 15, 2026 ('inside the rise of TJ Maxx'); Motley Fool, Jan 15, 2026 ('TJX ... benefits from tariffs and inflation').
- Venture and PE money in liquidation marketplaces: Highstock $30M Series A led by a16z (https://a16z.com/announcement/investing-in-highstock/; WWD, Sept 10, 2026); B-Stock $65M from Spectrum Equity (FinSMEs, 2018).
- Informal market exists: Business Insider (Sept 2, 2022) reported a 22-year-old with a seven-figure business reselling abandoned cargo, and (Dec 2, 2021) that abandoned containers attract opportunistic buyers.

Pain on the carrier and forwarder side:
- The Loadstar (2019, https://theloadstar.com/abandoned-containers-who-pays-forwarders-it-could-be-you/): forwarders often bear liability when a customer disappears or goes insolvent, and carriers only lien-sell resalable cargo.
- Legal mechanics confirm the need for a specialist: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/19/141.11 (right to make entry) and https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/19/127.1 (General Order).

Counter-evidence: US container imports were falling through 2025-26 (Los Angeles Times, Nov 2025; gCaptain on NRF, Dec 2025), so yard and demurrage pressure may be lower than the idea claims.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not position this as a cargo marketplace or a buy-and-flip desk, where you compete with carrier lien sales, open General Order auctions and Storage-Wars-style resellers. Sell it as a fee-based 'estate customs desk' to the parties who hold the pain and the cash but lack customs know-how:

1. Bankruptcy trustees and assignees for the benefit of creditors, for Southern California importer failures.
2. Asset-based lenders and factors with liens on in-transit inventory.
3. Carriers and NVOCCs, who want the box gone with the demurrage claim settled.

Bundle two services that no liquidator, marketplace or refund-claim buyer combines. First, file the estate's IEEPA refund claims as importer of record, since the estate is often the refund claimant. Second, rescue the estate's stranded containers: title, carrier certificate, entry and compliance screening. Charge a success fee on incremental estate recovery plus a flat per-box handling fee, with the buyer pre-funding duties. Keep the desk as a licensed broker or services firm and avoid inventory risk.

Start narrow, in categories with low compliance risk (soft goods, non-children's home goods) and high value per container. Refuse boxes needing CPSC, FDA or FCC certification and boxes with UFLPA exposure. Use the CBP General Order sale as the fallback price floor, so you only take boxes where you clearly beat it on timing or recovery.

Before building, validate three things:
1. Ask 5 carrier or NVOCC demurrage desks how many resalable orphaned boxes they see per month and how they dispose of them today. This tests the biggest risk, that carriers already handle the good ones.
2. Ask 3 Chapter 7 trustees or ABL lenders whether they would pay a success fee for this.
3. Confirm with a licensed broker that carriers will issue release certificates to a purchaser-IOR on non-negotiable bills.

This verdict rests on about 20 direct fetches of named vendor pages plus background knowledge, and several key sites returned 503 or 403 (Aidin, Ensocare, Central Logic, ACEP, GCAL). Main risks: OpenBeds already sells to state behavioral health authorities in 52 states and territories and could add a 'verified criteria' layer. Facilities may refuse or resent AI intake-line calls. State call-recording and AI-disclosure rules apply. Stale or wrong rules could cause clinical harm and liability. RHTP money flows through state plans, so sales cycles are slow.

Permitted uses include IT infrastructure, technology and AI adoption, and substance use disorder and mental health treatment services, so the funding source is real: https://www.medicaid.gov/resources-for-states/rural-health. The page says nothing about vendor procurement, and I could not verify the claim that every state has posted RHTP funding opportunities. (2) States already pay for behavioral health bed visibility. OpenBeds is claimed in 52 states and territories (https://bamboohealth.com/solutions/openbeds/, redirected from openbeds.net). Juvare announced a California statewide behavioral health bed capacity visibility partnership on Sept 1, 2026 (https://www.juvare.com/thought-leadership/news/juvare-partners-with-california-to-strengthen-statewide-behavioral-health-bed-capacity-visibility/). result.sharper_angle: Do not pitch it as a better bed registry, because OpenBeds and Juvare already sell to states. Sell it as a verified-rules layer: a nightly voice-agent audit of how receiving facilities actually behave, scored against what the registry says, with the named decider and a script. Sequence it in three steps. (1) Start with one rural region and one high-pain vertical, pediatric and adolescent psychiatric placement, where the exclusions are unwritten and ED boarding is worst. Sell to critical access hospital EDs and the state hospital association or rural health office, funded from RHTP behavioral health or IT lines. Start with the founder nurse's binder and use the voice agent to keep it current rather than to build it from nothing. (3) Longer term, offer receiving facilities a listing to pre-qualify referrals, and pitch the data to registry vendors (Bamboo, Juvare) as an accuracy feed or an acquisition target. Before building, validate two things I could not: that a few receiving-unit supervisors will answer an AI or human-assisted call and share their rules on the record, and that the registries do not already capture these criteria. result.white_space: No product found that does what this idea describes: a landlord-side tracker mapping each voucher unit to a PHA-specific rent-adjustment window, then generating and logging the request. Product Hunt search returned no Section 8 landlord products, GitHub search returned zero repos, and no vendor homepage checked advertised the feature. The unserved gap is a per-PHA rules database (notice window, form or email channel, eligibility gates) for small voucher landlords, small PM firms, or turnkey and investor-PM channels lacking this workflow. Caveat: the 200-call WebSearch budget was already exhausted, so the competitor sweep used direct page fetches only. Absence of competitors is a weaker finding than usual, and a manual Crunchbase, YC and Google check is still needed before building. The premise is also shakier than the idea states. CMHA's landlord FAQ (https://www.cmha.net/housing/landlords/landlord_faq.php) describes a rolling process, not a once-a-year forfeiture. Requests go by email to RentAdjustment@cmha.net, and the effective date is the 1st of the month after 60 days from receipt. The HAP contract must be at least one year old, a passed annual inspection is needed within 12 months of the effective date, at least 12 months must have passed since the last approved adjustment, the request must be signed by landlord and tenant, and the amount must be rent-reasonable. At CMHA a missed window costs some months, not a full year, and a higher payment standard does not by itself justify a higher rent because rent reasonableness caps the request. The forfeit-a-year claim comes from one forum post that itself warns that HUD publishing a number is not the same as your authority paying it and that each PHA adopts its own schedule. It may be true in some PHAs and false in others, so it needs validation per authority. The business model is also weak: the value is one action per unit per year, so retention after the first cycle is doubtful, the $5 per unit per month fee is small, and the success fee is hard to attribute because a landlord can send one email once shown the rules.
result.evidence_of_demand: Weak. The idea's own source is one BiggerPockets thread, Section 8 rents went up for FY2027. Most landlords won't collect it (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1301792-section-8-rents-went-up-for-fy2027-most-landlords-wont-collect-it). It had 1 upvote, 6 replies and 902 views. The author is a professional Memphis operator (few hundred doors, mostly Section 8, owns a management company), not a small landlord asking for a tool, and the post has no product pitch. One commenter said anything tied to a lease anniversary should go in one tracker with the notice deadline counted back, which signals a DIY spreadsheet or calendar habit, not spend. Other commenters warned that fighting for the last 30 dollars a month risks a 60-day vacancy and that tenants resist increases because their share rises. The other two BiggerPockets threads cited in the idea (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302305-furnace-and-water-heater-on-wood-platforms-cleveland-section-8-inspection and https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302138-how-realistic-is-it-to-raise-rents-100-on-existing-tenants) mention no tool, deadline-tracking need or willingness to pay. The Cleveland thread is about a furnace inspection problem. No RFPs, no evidence of existing spend on workarounds and no regulation forcing spend were found. Mild positive signals: PHAs run recurring landlord briefings (SLHA, https://www.slha.org/partner-with-slha/landlords/), so the audience is reachable, and CMHA still handles requests by email with strict eligibility gates, so there is manual friction to remove. Overall this is a plausible pain, not a validated purchase.
result.kill_reason: n/a. No direct funded competitor or dominant incumbent was found, so the verdict is gap, not crowded or dominated. It is a marginal gap: the pain is real but thin (one forum thread), the forfeit-a-year premise looks overstated for at least CMHA, and the recurring-revenue model is weak. Web search was capped, so the competitor sweep was limited and the founder should validate before building.
result.sharper_angle: Do not build a generic deadline-tracker SaaS. Sell a per-PHA voucher rent-adjustment audit and filing service instead of a subscription. The landlord or PM uploads a rent roll and HAP contracts and gets a per-unit report of the collectible increase after PHA rules and rent reasonableness. It shows which units are eligible now and prepares the PHA-specific packet (form or email, tenant and landlord signatures), for a flat fee or a percentage of the first-year captured increase. Chain the deadlines the way the PHA does: CMHA requires a passed inspection within 12 months of the effective date, at least 12 months since the last adjustment, and a rent-reasonable amount, so one tool should track inspection readiness, rent-reasonableness comps and the rent-adjustment window together. That bundle is worth more than a calendar reminder, and it connects to the inspection failures seen in the Cleveland thread. Distribute through channels that already hold voucher doors: turnkey and investor-PM firms in Memphis, Cleveland and St. Louis, plus PHA landlord briefings, selling a per-door white-label add-on before selling to individual landlords. Hand-build rules for 3 PHAs and verify the forfeit premise against each PHA's actual policy (rolling request versus anniversary-tied) before writing any software.

Important caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before my first query, so none of the 6-12 planned searches ran. I checked only about 20 direct page fetches. Many returned 404, 503, 403 or DNS errors, and Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch and Product Hunt could not be checked. This verdict is therefore low confidence. Within that limit, no company found sells a fixed-sum, instant payout triggered by a mandatory evacuation order. What exists is adjacent: post-event philanthropic cash (GiveDirectly), free lodging (Airbnb.org), slow claim-based FEMA aid, and receipt-based ALE and civil-authority cover that is tied to a covered peril and a state of emergency (verified for California, Ins. Code 2060(c)). The unserved wedge is a no-receipt cash benefit for the pre-claim cost of leaving. It would target renters and hourly workers, and cover evacuations with no property damage (for example, precautionary hurricane surge-zone orders). Delivery would go through employers, credit unions or municipalities.

Risks that decide viability: insurance licensing and rate filing state by state; adverse selection, since people buy when a storm is in the cone (expect binding moratoria and waiting periods); data access to evacuation zones (Genasys, county GIS, inconsistent zone-letter ordering); catastrophic correlation, since a single hurricane orders out an entire book at once and needs real reinsurance; and small-ticket unit economics ($3-15 per month, with 15-25% commission).

result.sharper_angle: Skip the consumer app and the insurance license at the start. Sell an 'evacuation stipend' to employers of hourly workers in surge and wildfire zones (hospitals, nursing homes, hotels, grocers) and to cities and philanthropies. It is a pre-funded fixed payout triggered by the legal evacuation order, with payment by FedNow or RTP. Employers have their own reasons to pay: staff who leave safely come back to work, and staffing plans improve if workers can afford to go. Cities gain compliance and lives saved. Start as an administered employer benefit or a philanthropic anticipatory-cash program in the GiveDirectly mold, with a reserve or fronted capacity and no retail policies. Once the trigger data and payout rails are proven on one or two counties, layer on a licensed MGA and fronting carrier for group policies, then individual renter policies. The moat is not the payout speed. It is exclusive or clean access to address-level evacuation-order feeds and an employer or municipal distribution channel that avoids consumer adverse selection.

result.white_space:
The core claim 'buyers cannot currently buy orphaned cargo' is wrong. About ten US salvage buyers (Salvex, United Liquidations, Salvage Groups and others) already buy abandoned boxes from carriers and forwarders and resell them, and carriers already run lien sales. A commodity 'buy boxes at port and flip' desk is a crowded, thin-margin business. The Businessweek example firm makes roughly GBP 500k on 5-10 containers a week.

The gap I could find is narrower and rests partly on things competitor sites do not mention, so it is unproven:
- **Legally tangled, high-value branded cargo.** These are boxes with the bill of lading in a dead importer's name, a trustee and a carrier lien in play, and compliance exposure (CPSC, FCC, FDA, UFLPA, IPR). Salvage buyers work AS-IS and push entry, duties and logistics onto the buyer, and their public pages do not describe solving title, importer-of-record and compliance together.
- **A trustee-facing offer.** None of the salvage buyers advertises one. Liquidators have the trustee relationships but no cargo-at-port capability that I could find.
- **Broker-grade entry plumbing.** This means a single-transaction bond, purchaser-as-importer-of-record, ACE entry and pre-screening of what is legal to sell. Only a licensed customs broker can offer it credibly.
- **Carrier waiver leverage under the FMC billing rule (46 CFR Part 541).** Carriers may bill only the party that contracted for carriage, and that party is now an insolvent estate. The carrier's real collection options are therefore the lien and cargo disposal, which strengthens a trade-a-waiver-for-removal pitch. This is inference from the rule, not tested.

Two risks to the wedge. First, right to make entry needs a genuine financial interest, and a nominal consignee or document-holder does not qualify (19 CFR Part 141, subpart B; CBP ruling H242069, whose text I could not fetch). The purchaser-as-IOR model must be structured with real title and purchase, not a service arrangement. Second, established liquidators could add a cargo module using their existing networks.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Real demand for an abandoned-cargo fix is documented, but I found no direct proof that anyone pays for a 'rescue desk' as specified.

Evidence that the pain and spend exist:
- TT Club StopLoss guidance 'TTC SL23 Abandoned Cargo' (updated Nov 2024) says abandonment 'creates considerable costs on container demurrage, detention, storage and disposal' and demands 'significant management resource'. It is aimed at forwarders, NVOCCs and terminals: https://www.ttclub.com/news-and-resources/publications/article/stoploss-abandonment-of-cargo/
- Carriers and salvage buyers already transact in this space. Bloomberg Businessweek (2021) reports cargo-salvage buyers either pay for containers or charge a fee to dispose of them, and Salvex has a dedicated 'transportation abandonment' director: https://www.jeffwise.net/2021/11/30/businessweek-when-shipping-containers-are-abandoned-the-cargo-becomes-a-mystery-prize/
- Demurrage and storage costs run at $75-$300+ per container per day (https://www.freightamigo.com/en/blog/logistics/understanding-demurrage-strategies-to-minimize-fees-in-global-shipping/). GO warehouse storage runs about $50-$150 per day, plus transfer fees of $950-$1,350 (search summary of https://docshipper.com/glossary/general-order-customs-definition-logistics/).
- Statutory clock: 15 days to entry, then General Order, then sale after about 6 months (19 CFR 127: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-19/chapter-I/part-127; https://www.pcbusa.com/post/the-cbp-and-cargo-abandonment).
- 2025-26 stress on small importers: https://www.seatrade-maritime.com/regulations/tariffs-stall-us-importers-small-businesses-warn-of-bankruptcy. The Feb 2026 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling and the CAPE refund portal (live Apr 20, 2026) created about $166B of refund claims, and bankruptcy estates are monetizing them (American Signature sold about $7.25M): https://www.mondaq.com/unitedstates/insolvencybankruptcy/1816290/tariffs-turmoil-and-tax-refunds-turning-uncle-sams-iou-into-cash-in-bankruptcy and https://fortune.com/2026/04/20/cape-tariff-refund-portal-small-business-challenges/
- Suppliers are actively marketing tariff-driven cargo buyouts: https://unitedliquidations.com/solutions/abandoned-refused-container-resolution/

Weak points:
- Volume is unproven. A '700,000 loaded containers abandoned per year in the US (DOT)' claim appears in blog snippets, but I could not verify it and it looks unreliable.
- I found no data on how many failed importers leave cargo with a trustee, and no RFP, forum thread or trustee demand signal.
- Salvage margins look modest.
result.kill_reason: n/a. The commodity version of this idea is crowded and not worth building, but a narrow wedge (broker-grade title, entry and compliance for legally tangled, high-value orphaned cargo, sourced from trustees and stuck NVOCCs) is not visibly served. Salvex pushes entry to the buyer, and United Liquidations' page never mentions entry, importer-of-record or trustees. Proceed only if the pivot below is validated cheaply first.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not present it as a marketplace or a flip desk, because that is Salvex, United Liquidations and the Salvage Groups. Make it a customs-broker-run 'abandoned-cargo resolution agent' with three differences:

1. **Sell to the stuck party, not the buyer.**
   - The paying customers are NVOCCs, freight forwarders and carriers' demurrage desks, who hold the lien and liability and are exposed under TT Club-style guidance, plus bankruptcy trustees and assignees.
   - Charge a flat resolution fee or a share of recovered value. The trustee, not the off-price buyer, is the client.
   - Keep the salvage and liquidator firms as outlets for junk boxes, not as competitors.

2. **Take only legally complex, compliance-screened, branded cargo.**
   - Cargo that salvage buyers avoid is your lane: a dead consignee, a bill of lading in a bankrupt name, and CPSC, FCC, FDA, UFLPA or IPR risk.
   - Advertise that you handle title transfer, carrier lien release, the single-transaction bond, purchaser-as-IOR entry and pre-screening as one package, in days, not months.
   - Structure real purchaser financial interest to satisfy right-to-make-entry, and get a customs attorney to review it before the first deal.

3. **Use the FMC billing rule as leverage.** Under 46 CFR Part 541, carriers can invoice only the contracting party. Build the standard 'remove the box in exchange for waiver and mitigation' offer around that, and package it as a repeatable playbook for carrier demurrage desks.

Validate before building: get 5-10 calls with NVOCC and forwarder claims managers and 2-3 Chapter 7 trustees in C.D. Cal. to confirm that legally stuck, high-value cargo exists in volume and that they would pay. Also confirm with a broker or attorney that purchaser-as-IOR works on these facts. If neither holds, the honest outcome is that this is just a small salvage business.

result.white_space:
The planning, calculator and decree-language layer is taken by DLA's CDLP network (1,000+ loan officers, a paid planning report, a free consumer site). A flat-fee planning desk would compete against free CDLP strategy sessions, so it should not be the core product. What looks unserved is narrower.

1. Execution of the assumption-with-release step. I found only advice on assumption. I found no firm that assembles the packet, tracks the servicer, chases release of liability and reports status to the attorney and the client. The CFPB documents servicers demanding refinances, months-long delays, repeated document requests and denials: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/homeowners-face-problems-with-mortgage-companies-after-divorce-or-death-of-a-loved-one/. Fannie Mae's servicing guide makes release of liability contingent on servicer and mortgage-insurer approval: https://servicing-guide.fanniemae.com/svc/f-1-17/processing-transfer-ownership. A servicer-by-servicer playbook and workflow is a data and operations asset that the CDLP model, which is commission-driven and loan-centric, does not provide.

2. New statutory rights that need help exercising. Maryland HB 1018 (effective Oct 1, 2025) makes conventional-loan assumption on divorce a right, applies retroactively to existing loans above FHA limits, and applies to decrees entered on or after that date: https://labor.maryland.gov/finance/advisories/advisory-ind-marylandlawmortgageassumptionupondivorce.shtml. Virginia HB 304 (July 1, 2026) and California AB 3100 (Jan 1, 2027) cover only newly originated loans, so they do not help the existing low-rate book. None of the three laws guarantees release of the departing spouse. Maryland, and FHA/VA/USDA loans nationwide, are therefore the addressable base for a release-focused execution service.

3. The assume-plus-second-lien sequence as one packaged workflow. Consumer content on HELOC buyouts is everywhere. DLA's public pages, the mortgage-info.com lender roundup, and Contour's guide do not describe a joint assumption-plus-second-lien product. That may be a gap in what I could fetch, so verify it with a few CDLP interviews.

4. A white-label or API layer for DIY-divorce platforms and mediation firms. Hello Divorce (over $5M raised) publishes guides and has no mortgage-execution product. Its guides send users to expert services.

Also unserved: the attorney-side deadline and enforcement tooling. An example is a release-deadline tracker with a fallback such as a forced refinance or sale. I did not find this offered as software.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Strong evidence that the problem is real and that professionals get paid for it. Weaker evidence that consumers will pay $495 to $995 to a new entrant.

Pain and regulation:
- The CFPB's Issue Spotlight on complaints from Dec 2021 to Aug 2024 documents servicers wrongly demanding refinances at today's rates, assumption delays of months or years, assumption denials for creditworthy spouses, and refusal to release original borrowers even when a decree requires it: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/homeowners-face-problems-with-mortgage-companies-after-divorce-or-death-of-a-loved-one/
- Three states legislated in response: Maryland HB 1018 (Oct 2025, retroactive to existing loans), Virginia HB 304 (July 2026) and California AB 3100 (Jan 2027, new loans only). Sources: https://natlawreview.com/article/ca-md-va-force-lenders-hand-divorce-triggered-mortgage-assumptions and https://infobytes.orrick.com/2024-09-27/california-enacts-mortgage-law-co-borrowing-divorces/
- Axios reported on how divorcees try to keep 3% mortgages: https://www.axios.com/2024/03/09/mortgage-rates-divorce. Practitioner blogs and law-firm posts about keeping a sub-4% rate are common.

Market size:
- The CDC counted 673,989 US divorces and annulments in 2022. Roughly 36% to 40% of divorces now involve people 50 or older (sources: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/dvs/marriage-divorce/national-marriage-divorce-rates-00-22.pdf, https://www.modernfamilylaw.com/resources/top-10-divorce-statistics-you-need-to-know/).
- No source I found gives the share of divorces with a below-4.5% first mortgage and a keeping spouse who qualifies alone. That number sets the real addressable market and needs its own estimate.

Existing spend and professional adoption:
- DLA claims 1,000+ CDLPs in all 50 states, a paid Divorce Mortgage Planning Report sold to attorneys and mediators, and $1,295 to $2,500 per-case advisory fees alongside commissions: https://www.divorcelendingassociation.com/practice_areas/cdlp-divorce-mortgage-planning-lending-certification-course.cfm
- CDFAs bill $150 to $450 an hour or flat fees from about $3,500: https://sandiegofamilymediation.com/what-does-it-cost-to-work-with-a-cdfa/ and https://www.feeonlynetwork.com/resources/certified-divorce-financial-analyst-cdfa/
- Hello Divorce has raised over $5M for DIY divorce and has in-house lending expertise: https://www.lawnext.com/2022/10/hello-divorce-raises-3-25m-to-span-more-of-the-divorce-lifecycle-including-financial-planning.html

Caveat: I found no evidence that consumers pay a standalone $495 to $995 fee for this. The proven payers are loan officers (commissions) and attorneys or mediators (report fees). I found no dedicated forum threads showing consumers asking for a paid execution service. The Bogleheads thread on release of liability after divorce was blocked by a paywall (HTTP 402), so its contents are unverified.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not build a divorce mortgage planner. That is the DLA and CDLP business, with 1,000+ loan officers giving away the analysis to win the loan, and a $495 to $995 planning fee would compete against free sessions.

Build assumption-and-release execution infrastructure for the people who already own the divorce relationship. Call it something like a release desk.

- **Product:** a per-case service that handles the servicer side. It builds the assumption and release-of-liability packet, applies a servicer-by-servicer playbook (required documents, timelines, mortgage-insurer approval, escalation paths including Reg X successor-in-interest and CFPB complaints), tracks the file to a signed release, and gives the attorney a dashboard and a decree-language and deadline generator.
- **Loan wedge:** start with the loans where assumption is a right or a norm. That means FHA, VA and USDA loans in every state, and Maryland conventional loans (decrees on or after Oct 1, 2025, retroactive to existing loans above FHA limits). Add Virginia and California as those laws phase in for newly originated loans.
- **Buyer:** the attorney, mediator, CDFA or DIY-divorce platform, paying per case or per seat, or a platform license. Consumers only see it through their professional. This avoids fee-splitting problems with attorneys and avoids competing with free CDLP consultations.
- **Financing:** stay unlicensed. Route the second-lien or HELOC step to CDLP loan officers and HELOC lenders under a compliant referral or co-marketing arrangement, so you complement DLA members. The optional NMLS-licensed broker layer can come later if the volume justifies it.
- **Data asset:** the servicer playbook database of assumption and release outcomes (time to release, denial reasons, required documents). It compounds with every case, and neither DLA's planning report nor lender blogs provide it.

**Validation before building.**
1. Interview 10 to 15 CDLPs and 10 family-law attorneys or mediators. Ask who does the servicer chase today, whether they get paid for it, and what release rates look like.
2. Run 5 to 10 live FHA, VA or Maryland cases for free to measure real servicer behavior and turnaround.
3. Check whether Hello Divorce or a similar DIY platform would license a mortgage-execution module.
4. Confirm the wedge is not already a paid add-on inside the Divorce Mortgage Planning Report.
5. Estimate the size of the assumable and Maryland segment, since it is a fraction of the roughly 674K annual divorces.

result.white_space:
Nobody I found sells a shared, pooled, live remote-RN witness subscription to critical access hospitals. The specific gaps are:
(1) Live human supply. MidasVIEW replaces the second person with recorded video reviewed later. Pyxis remote witness still needs a colleague on shift. Virtual-nursing vendors cover admissions, discharges, sitters and documentation. Remote pharmacy vendors cover order verification. Nobody provides a licensed second person on demand at 3am.
(2) Transfusion, high-alert and pediatric double-checks. Asynchronous video cannot substitute for a live independent check before administration. Remote IDC is documented as feasible but under-evidenced, and only a few institutions do it (ONS 2024).
(3) Small-hospital fit. MidasVIEW pilots are at tertiary and children's hospitals. Small facilities lag on diversion controls: only 57% of single facilities actively monitor camera footage, and CAHs lack pharmacy staff to review video the next day.
(4) Insurer-linked audit trail. No diversion vendor sells to liability or captive insurers.
The wedge is narrow and time-limited. Avel eCare, VirtuAlly and the telepharmacy vendors could add a witness line quickly, and MidasVIEW could add live witness routing.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Pain is well documented. Willingness to pay for this specific service is not, and I found no RFPs, forum posts asking for a paid remote witness, or vendor pricing.
Pain evidence:
- Bluesight 2026 Hospital Pharmacy Operations Report (437 respondents): about 63% of leaders reported at least one diversion event in the past year. https://bluesight.com/news/bluesight-releases-2026-hospital-pharmacy-and-privacy-reports/
- Peer-reviewed: "a significant barrier to the destruction of controlled substances was the availability of a second witness", worst on overnight shifts. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11392538
- Peer-reviewed: waste stream is "one of the weakest links in the controlled substance chain of custody". https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8958124/
- Survey of US hospital pharmacies: smaller single facilities lag on diversion controls, and only 57.1% actively monitor camera footage. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11676067/
- Nurse and staffing sources note that "virtual waste", where the witness signs without watching, is a known diversion tactic, and that some rural facilities have only one licensed person on nights so techs co-sign. https://www.medicalsolutions.com/blog/clinician/narcotic-waste/ and https://www.myamericannurse.com/drug-diversion-in-healthcare/
Money and regulatory signals:
- MIDAS raised outside capital for video-witness waste (a $2M Series A extension in 2023), so some investors see a market. https://www.newswire.com/news/midas-healthcare-solutions-extends-series-a-round-with-new-investment-22156357
- Rural Health Transformation Program: $50B over 2026-2030, about $200M average first-year award per state, with virtual nursing and workforce named as aligned uses. https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/press-releases/cms-announces-50-billion-awards-strengthen-rural-health-all-50-states and https://avasure.com/blog/rhtp-how-virtual-care-can-benefit-rural-hospitals/
- Massachusetts allowed a virtual two-person count and disposal waiver for its long-term-care Medication Administration Program, provided an in-person count happens at least every 7 days. This shows regulators can accept virtual witnessing in limited settings. https://www.mass.gov/doc/map-virtual-two-person-count-and-disposal-of-countable-controlled-substances-waiver-notice/download
Counter-evidence and risks:
- Some state rules require both people to personally witness destruction, for example Ohio Admin. Code 4729:5-3-01. The rule text I saw covers disposal generally and I did not confirm how it applies to point-of-care waste. https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-4729:5-3-01
- Remote double-check evidence is thin. https://www.ons.org/publications-research/voice/news-views/04-2024/remote-independent-double-check-has-benefits-we-need
- Cheaper substitutes exist: async video review, or a tech or supervisor co-sign.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not lead with live remote witnessing of narcotic waste. MidasVIEW's async video review already competes on that use case, and state or board rules may block live remote witnessing in some places. Reposition as a live "second licensed person on demand" service for critical access hospitals, sold as a pooled night-shift subscription. Lead with what video review cannot replace:
1. Transfusion verification, high-alert double-checks (insulin, heparin) and pediatric dosing, each needing a live independent check before administration.
2. Waste witnessing as a bundled add-on. Use a $150 tablet that records every event so the hospital gets the audit trail, with the live RN taking the call when no colleague is free.
Go to market through channels that already hold CAH night-shift trust rather than selling cold to 1,300 CAHs:
- White-label or partner with Avel eCare, VirtuAlly, Teledigm, or CPS/Cardinal remote pharmacy. Pharmacists are eligible witnesses too, so a pharmacist-plus-RN pool widens supply.
- Pilot in one Nurse Licensure Compact state with a written board of pharmacy and nursing opinion in hand before the first sale.
- Sell the audit log to the hospital's liability or captive insurer, and pay for pilots from a state Rural Health Transformation workforce or quality grant.
Before building, get two or three CAH pharmacy directors or CNOs to sign a paid pilot letter. Also confirm that P&T policy plus state rules allow live video witnessing. Willingness to pay is the least-proven part.
