result.white_space:
Verdict is gap, and a narrower one than the pitch implies. No product found does the specific loop the idea describes: proof of US-person status, the attribute written to an IdP through SCIM, enforcement in Drive, GitHub and PLM, and continuous drift detection. Four things fill the space today. IDV vendors (Persona, Incode, Socure, Nametag, CLEAR, Entra Verified ID) prove someone is real but do not assert or record ITAR eligibility. archTIS NC Protect enforces nationality-based access but only inside Microsoft 365 and file shares, and it trusts whatever attribute it is given. Managed-service shops (BEMO at about $4,800/month, ATX CMMC Space plus $30/user/month) deliver it as consulting with 8-month timelines. PLM vendors enforce access to an admin-typed attribute that no one has proven.

What is genuinely unserved:
- A lightweight, startup-priced system of record for US-person and permitted-data-category status, with the Empowered Official sign-off, that syncs to Okta, Entra and Google Workspace groups.
- Continuous deemed-export exposure scanning across the Drive, GitHub, Slack and PLM permission lists that startups actually use. Many are on commercial Google Workspace, which is not ITAR-compliant, and they cannot afford a GCC High or enclave migration.
- A managed workflow for licensed or TAA-scoped foreign-person exceptions, which is where hiring friction really sits.

Parts of the pitch that are not white space:
- Supplier KYB and counterfeit screening is owned by Exiger, Kharon and Sayari.
- CMMC evidence packs are owned by Secureframe, Vanta and Drata.
- Candidate and DPRK fraud detection is crowded and moving fast (Persona, Incode, Socure, Nametag, Endorsed).

Biggest structural risks:
1. The 'why now' is broken. DoD suspended CMMC Phase 2, due 10 Nov 2026, on 13 Jul 2026 and launched a 60-day reform review. Phase 1 self-assessments remain. Do not build the go-to-market around a Nov 2026 CMMC cliff.
2. Legal and product risk. The Clifford Chance settlement ($132K) shows DOJ IER penalizes employers who over-apply ITAR into citizenship discrimination. ITAR does not require hiring only US persons. Under INA 274B, employers cannot demand specific documents or run citizenship checks unevenly. A biometric 'US person' scanner sold to HR is legally delicate. Verifying green-card, asylee and refugee status by document scan is harder than a citizen passport check, and the I-9 already exists as the system of record.
3. Easy DIY. An IT admin can put an I-9-derived flag into an Okta group, so the paid value must be audit and drift detection plus the exception workflow, not the attribute itself.
4. Coverage limit. WebSearch is US-only and Crunchbase and YC searches surfaced nothing, so a stealth or very early startup on this exact wedge cannot be ruled out.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Real spend and regulatory pressure exist, but I found no direct evidence that anyone pays for a US-person identity attribute as a standalone product. I found no RFPs, forum threads or Reddit complaints asking for one.

Enforcement pressure:
- DDTC fined BAE Systems $36M in Aug 2026 (half suspended, 3-year consent agreement). Violations included unlicensed technical-data exports to China and Canada: https://exportcompliancedaily.com/article/2026/08/14/ddtc-fines-bae-systems-36-m-for-export-violations-stemming-from-compliance-issues-2608130044?BC=bc_6a7e5b887dca1
- Legal commentary says space startups often first meet ITAR when they try to hire foreign nationals: https://spacenews.com/op-ed-attention-silicon-valley-the-exposure-of-space-startups-to-us-export-control-rules/ and https://newspaceeconomy.ca/2026/09/11/are-u-s-space-export-controls-protecting-technology-or-surrendering-overseas-markets/
- Compliance guidance repeatedly warns that I-9 proves work authorization, not export-control status, and that Google Drive and Dropbox are not ITAR-compliant: https://www.myisoconsultants.com/post/understanding-itar-compliance-verifying-us-person-status-my-iso-consultants and https://casrai.org/guides/us-person-status-foreign-national-access

Existing spend on workarounds:
- BEMO managed ITAR/CMMC IT costs about $4,800/month: https://www.bemopro.com/compliance-requirements/itar-background-check
- ATX CMMC Space is $299/user/month, plus $30/user/month for ITAR: https://atxdefense.com/capabilities/cmmc-compliance/

result.white_space: Nobody found does the specific thing. Across roughly 20 searches, no startup, product, or open-source tool uses voice agents to phone receiving psychiatric units and specialty hospitals on a schedule and record their tacit acceptance rules, the name and hours of the decision-maker, and the script that works. The unserved wedge is real but narrow. (1) Registries (OpenBeds, BHL, state portals) capture bed counts and formal criteria through facility self-report. The 2019 ASPE and Psychiatric Services work found no state registry linked to EHR or ADT data, and respondents rated registry accuracy and timeliness poor. Only NC has hourly automation, and that is bed count, not rule extraction. (2) Nobody delivers a ranked call list plus script by SMS to a rural ER charge nurse. Registries are portals that still end in 'call the facility'. (3) The hardest-to-place groups are children, autism and IDD, aggression, medically complex, out-of-state Medicaid. Boarding research shows these patients wait longest, and generic registry filters handle them worst. (4) Decline reasons and real decision-makers are not aggregated across facilities anywhere. Not unserved: bed availability, digital referrals, and generic outbound voice AI. Also not a clean white space: stroke, trauma and OB, where hospital-run transfer centers and TeleTracking, Central Logic and RelateCare already own the workflow.
result.evidence_of_demand: Problem demand is strong. Payment demand for this specific product is unproven, and I found no RFP, vendor contract, or customer purchase for an acceptance-rule intelligence service. Evidence: (1) Boarding is a documented, costly crisis. Among about 1.4M national pediatric mental health ED visits ending in admission or transfer, 13.1% lasted 24 hours or more (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12159435/). Prolonged boarders were mostly declined by all state inpatient units (69%) and were more often under 12, on Medicaid or uninsured, or had neurodevelopmental disorders (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33279330). Only 38% of rural and remote EDs have designated transfer guidelines for children with mental health issues. A 14-year-old was boarded 42 days. NPR 2025: https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2025/08/15/nx-s1-5502689/pediatric-mental-health-er-boarding-jama-health-forum. Interhospital transfer acceptance falls with boarding and census, especially in rural settings (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12120653/). (2) Registry limits are documented. ASPE/Psychiatric Services found manual updates, no EHR link, and 'poor' accuracy ratings (https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/migrated_legacy_files/190716/IPBedTrack.pdf, https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ps.201900079). The Washington locator says to still call the facility to arrange transfer. (3) Money is flowing. States buy registries. NC launched BH SCAN, Michigan a registry dashboard, Montana had a 2025 legislative item to adopt an electronic bed registry (https://www.dphhs.mt.gov/assets/2025Legislature/BHSFG-09-Adopt-ElectronicBedRegistryandEnhance.pdf, page returned 404 on my fetch so treat as unverified). RHTP is $50B over five years, about $10B per year, with state awards of $147M to $281M and up to 10% allowed for tech pilots (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/press-releases/cms-announces-50-billion-awards-strengthen-rural-health-all-50-states; https://shvs.org/resources/may-2026-state-implementation-of-the-rural-health-transformation-program-ramps-up/). Kentucky's RHTP telebehavioral hub includes 'shared reporting and registry functions' (https://www.chfs.ky.gov/agencies/os/oas/Documents/RHT%20Telebehavioral%20Health%20Support%20-%20RFA.pdf). Behavioral health boarding, crisis, and tele-behavioral projects are funded in KY, NE, TN. (4) Comparable spend on a similar model exists. Aidin and CarePort get paid for facility-criteria-based referral matching in post-acute, and voice-AI directory verification is an emerging paid category. Caveats: RHTP money is going mostly to crisis facilities, tele-behavioral and workforce, and I saw no state line item for placement intelligence. Critics call RHTP funds a band-aid (https://lexingtonky.news/2026/08/31/critics-say-rural-health-transformation-program-funds-are-a-band-aid-that-comes/). The $300-600 per ER per month price is an unsupported assumption.
result.sharper_angle: Narrow it and re-position it as the verification layer under existing registries, not a rival registry. (1) Start with one hard, measurable slice: pediatric and IDD/autism psychiatric placement for rural EDs in a single state, where boarding days are already reported and Medicaid or the children's behavioral health agency feels the cost. Drop stroke, trauma and OB, which TeleTracking, Central Logic and RelateCare own. (2) Sell 'ground truth' rather than another portal. Run a nightly call program that measures actual acceptance behavior (accept and decline rates by population, real decision-maker, hours, working script) and sell it to state agencies and hospital associations as a QA and boarding-reduction service, and as a data feed or partner integration to OpenBeds, Behavioral Health Link and the state bed portals. Their weakness is self-reported data, so co-opt them instead of racing them. (3) Keep humans in the loop. Start with human or hybrid callers, because intake nurses may refuse to talk to bots or may not disclose exclusions to one, and the calls only cover facility rules with no patient data. Measure willingness to answer before building an SMS product. (4) Handle legal risk up front. Publishing explicit exclusions like 'no autism' invites ADA and Section 504 disputes and facility pushback. Show ER users a private acceptance-likelihood score, the decision-maker and the script, and keep raw exclusion text non-public. Use SMS only with de-identified, patient-free queries or move to a HIPAA-compliant channel. (5) Prove it before selling it. Use the founder-nurse binder as a seed and run a 60-80 facility pilot, with pre and post placement time and call counts at five ERs, before approaching RHTP offices. Fastest kill test: in the first two weeks, check that at least 60% of intake lines will give rule answers to a voice agent, and that a state buyer will name a budget line."

result.white_space: The reminder and calendar layer is not open. RentsPaid, HAPSecure and TenantKeep already ship anniversary or rent-increase-window alerts at free to $39/mo, and TenantKeep advertises PHA letter generation. A plain tracker with alerts would be a fourth entrant selling against free. All of them are software-only and unfunded. What remains unserved is (1) actually filing the request and chasing it to approval, since TenantKeep says outright that it does not file; (2) a human-verified, authority-by-authority rulebook (window length, form, portal versus mail, comps requirement, tenant signature) in the Section 8-heavy investor markets: Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis, Indianapolis; VoucherReady explicitly declines to supply PHA numbers; (3) contingency pricing tied to captured increase, when every competitor charges flat SaaS or free; (4) a portfolio leakage audit for small PM firms and out-of-state investors (units at or under the new payment standard with no filed request). Two caveats. Payment standard increases apply to the family's subsidy at the next regular reexam (24 CFR 982.505), not at the lease anniversary, so the pitch conflates two clocks. Rent reasonableness also caps the gain, and BiggerPockets commenters note many voucher units are already at the local maximum.
result.evidence_of_demand: Weak-to-moderate, mostly indirect. Nobody was found paying for this specific outcome. (1) The source BiggerPockets post says most landlords will not collect the FY2027 increase because of the 60-day-before-anniversary window (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1301792-section-8-rents-went-up-for-fy2027-most-landlords-wont-collect-it). Commenters there recommend dedicated notice-deadline trackers and warn 'Agencies lose paperwork more than people think', and Memphis owners confirm the 60-day written notice plus rent-reasonableness approval. No commenter named a tool or service. (2) At least three small startups (RentsPaid, HAPSecure, TenantKeep) are building for the exact customer, and HAPSecure charges $39/$99/$249 per month with pay-per-use extras. That shows a paid price point exists for Section 8 compliance software, and that founders see demand (https://hapsecure.app/). (3) PHA request windows vary from 60 to 120 days and by form and portal, which is real complexity: https://www.gcrealtyinc.com/blog/requesting-a-section-8-rent-increase. Section 8-focused PM firms and PHAs publish step-by-step guides for it. (4) A separate thread shows friction with tenant signatures and paperwork (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1073997-section-8-tenant-refuses-to-sign-rent-increase-form). Not found: RFPs, regulations forcing spend, forum threads of landlords who lost a year of increase and paid to fix it, or any funded company. The claim of 'real money left uncollected' rests on one forum post.
result.sharper_angle: Do not build a tracker: RentsPaid (free) and HAPSecure ($39/mo) already ship the alert, and TenantKeep advertises letter generation. Build a done-for-you rent-increase filing service on contingency pricing, with no monthly SaaS fee and about 50 to 100 percent of the first month of the approved increase as the fee. The landlord uploads the HAP contract and lease. You verify the anniversary, pull comps, prepare the PHA-specific packet, submit it by portal, mail or certified mail, and chase it to approval. Log every submission and contact so the landlord has proof if the PHA loses paperwork. Lead with a free 'unfiled increases' audit run on a rent roll plus HAP contracts, sold first to small PM firms and out-of-state investors in Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis and Indianapolis. The moat is the human-verified per-PHA rulebook and a track record of approvals, not the reminder software. Fold in a mid-lease correction request for wrong bedroom count or square footage. To de-risk, first check on 10 to 15 real units whether rent reasonableness and the payment-standard cap leave a meaningful increase. Also confirm that success fees are collectible from 1-to-50-unit owners once the PHA raises the rent on its own.

result.white_space: Verification is incomplete, so treat this as a provisional gap verdict, not a confirmed one. I found no product that pays a flat cash amount to an individual within hours because a mandatory evacuation order covers their address. Every adjacent player triggers on something else. Parametric platforms use physical measurements. FEMA and GiveDirectly pay after the event and need an application or a declaration. Homeowners and renters ALE and civil-authority cover is receipt-based. The unserved wedge is the legal-act trigger, paid out as a flat amount before the trip, to renters and hourly workers, funded by someone other than the individual (county or state emergency management, Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans, landlords or property managers, credit unions, philanthropy). That funder-pays model is the specific space I found nobody in. Main risks: a carrier could add a flat 'evacuation expense' rider to renters policies, and evacuation-zone data is held by vendors and counties, some under licensing terms that were not checked.
result.evidence_of_demand: Weak, and mostly unverified because the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) ran out before any of my searches ran. What I did verify by fetch: the Wikipedia hurricane-evacuation article says residents may decide against evacuating because of 'the monetary cost of evacuation' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_evacuation), and it cites no data or programs. The FEMA IHP page (https://www.fema.gov/assistance/individual/program) confirms that a federal cash program for uninsured 'serious needs' exists. That shows the need is recognised, but it is not evidence that individuals will pay $3-15 a month. From memory, and not verified: research on evacuation compliance repeatedly names cost and transportation as barriers, and California has moved to require faster advance payments of living-expense benefits after the January 2025 fires. Still to be checked: RFPs from county emergency-management agencies, Medicaid or Medicare Advantage disaster-transportation spend, employer disaster-relief funds, and any carrier filings for an evacuation-expense rider. The search budget needs to be raised to run those.
result.sharper_angle: Do not sell it to renters at $3-15 a month. Consumer micro-insurance has high customer-acquisition cost and heavy adverse selection: people buy when a named storm forms, and the El Nino burn-scar pitch is the moment risk is already known and hardest to price. The employer route also has a conflict. Hospitals, nursing homes and hotels often need essential staff to stay through an evacuation, so they will not want to pay staff to leave. The sharper version is an 'evacuation stipend' sold to funders that benefit from compliance and pay with pooled budgets. Buyers would be county and state emergency-management agencies, Medicaid managed-care and Medicare Advantage plans (for oxygen, dialysis or mobility-dependent members), landlords and property managers, and credit unions. The parametric contract turns an uncertain disaster budget into a fixed, pre-funded, per-address cash disbursement paid the moment an order posts, with a waiting period and a named-storm blackout to control adverse selection. Start with one hurricane-zone county or Medicaid plan, and offer it later as an embedded rider through renters carriers. The moat is the order-timestamp-to-payout pipeline plus licensed evacuation-zone data and compliance analytics, not the insurance wrapper. Before building, rerun the missing searches: Crunchbase and YC for 'evacuation' and 'parametric', carrier rider filings, and county RFPs.
